content: 1. Activities were conducted to identify evidence of infection in vectors. This included answering specific questions such as: Who was responsible for implementing entomological monitoring? At what level were these activities managed or coordinated? How were sites selected for monitoring, such as traps or human biting studies? If applicable, what mosquito species were included in the analysis, and what methods were used (e.g., dissection, PCR, L3 PCR)? What were the vector infection or infectivity rates, and what was the monthly or annual transmission potential? How were the results utilized? 2. If applicable, annex entomological monitoring reports should include detailed descriptions of surveillance activities, monitored indicators, and interpretations of the results. 3. Data on the number of patients with lymphedema or hydrocele is required. A brief narrative should describe the methodology used to identify these patients, including the year of the estimates. If possible, include a map showing the prevalence of filarial clinical disease by condition. Depending on the burden, this could include areas with and without cases or groupings by the number of cases. 4. A national overview of facilities providing morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) services should be included. Indicators should cover: The number of implementation units (IUs) with known patients. The number of IUs without known patients. The number of IUs with at least one facility designated to provide the recommended basic care package. The number of patients. The number of health facilities providing services. The number of health facilities surveyed to assess the quality of care. 5. For lymphedema and hydrocele, list the number of designated facilities providing services per IU with known patients. 6. Special circumstances affecting the implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of the program should be described. This may include issues such as: Stability or security concerns in the country. Immigration from LF-endemic countries, including nomadic populations or seasonal workers. 7. Resources and partnerships should be described briefly, including human resources involved in implementing the program and an estimate of financial resources utilized. For example, WHO financial and technical assistance for TAS in Region A. 8. A bibliography of all data sources used to develop the dossier should be included. This may consist of Ministry of Health records, published studies, academic theses, and other relevant documents. Key articles and reports should be noted and kept on file in the national program office. 9. A list of definitions for all abbreviations used in the dossier should be provided. 10. Validation is a new process endorsed by the global Strategic and Technical Advisory Group for Neglected Tropical Diseases, allowing WHO to officially acknowledge elimination as a public health problem. This process was recently applied to acknowledge the achievements of six countries that submitted dossiers in 2014 and 2015. Relevant questions raised by countries, partners, donors, and reviewers are presented to facilitate understanding, improve transparency, and assist LF elimination program managers. 11. Program managers should begin data gathering and archiving as early as possible and continue throughout the program. IU-level data should be updated annually as reports are submitted to WHO. Preparation of the dossier should begin once all endemic IUs have completed TAS1, allowing four years of post-MDA surveillance to document necessary data. 12. The dossier should be submitted in one of the six official UN working languages (Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, or Spanish). Countries should request WHO support if translation is required. 13. National program managers can request WHO to provide technical support for dossier preparation. WHO will coordinate technical support for requesting countries. Preparation of the dossier may require resources for data gathering and writing. Some programs have hired consultants to review, consolidate, and organize data and draft the narrative sections. 14. National program managers can submit a draft dossier to WHO for informal feedback. WHO will coordinate an informal review through the Regional Programme Review Group and provide feedback to enhance the dossier. 15. If supporting data are missing, the program should seek assistance from WHO. WHO has a large archive of reports and other files that may help identify missing data. If data cannot be found, key informants with accurate knowledge of the activities may provide insights. This should be reflected in the dossier narrative. 16. WHO aims to coordinate the review of the dossier and provide communication (acknowledgment or reasons for postponement) within six months to one year of submission. 17. If validation is postponed, WHO will provide feedback to identify specific concerns and guidance for addressing them. The national program should develop an activity plan to gather additional evidence, revise the dossier, and resubmit it for validation. 18. Validation may be postponed if required components of the dossier are not sufficiently addressed. Ensure all program data are well-documented, including endemicity, MDA requirements, MDA coverage, sentinel monitoring, TAS implementation, patient numbers, MMDP services, and post-validation surveillance commitments. 19. Countries should document the results of initial mapping surveys showing the proportion of infected individuals. If endemicity was determined using non-epidemiological data, ensure the data and methods are clearly presented. 20. In areas where lymphedema or hydrocele cases are found in non-endemic IUs, national LF elimination programs should analyze data carefully and consider re-evaluating endemicity. Care should be available for patients in these IUs. 21. The minimum package of care should be prioritized in districts with known patients. It is preferred that care is available in all areas mapped as endemic, even if no cases have been identified. 22. Basic care should be available for all lymphedema and/or hydrocele patients from an endemic country, regardless of the cause of morbidity. 23. In areas of W. bancrofti, hydrocele surgery should be available at least at tertiary facilities. Lymphedema management should include hygiene, skin care, and prevention of acute attacks.
